nameStory: The broadleaf arrowhead gets its name from its distinctive arrow-shaped leaves that look like they could have been crafted by a skilled archer. The 'broadleaf' part distinguishes it from its narrow-leaved cousins, as this species shows off the widest, most dramatic arrowhead shape in the family. It's like nature's perfect arrow pointing up from the water's edge!
description: Broadleaf arrowhead is a striking wetland plant that grows 1-4 feet tall along pond edges, marshes, and slow streams throughout New England. Its most recognizable feature is its bold, arrow-shaped leaves that emerge directly from the water or wet soil on long stalks. In summer, it sends up separate flowering stalks topped with clusters of bright white, three-petaled flowers that stand out beautifully against the green foliage. This native aquatic plant forms colonies through underground tubers and has been an important food source for centuries.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive arrow-shaped leaves with three pointed lobes - one pointing up and two pointing backward like barbs. The leaves feel smooth and slightly waxy, emerging on separate stalks directly from the base with no central stem.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white flowers with three rounded petals arranged in whorls of three along a separate stalk. Each flower is about an inch across with a bright yellow center, and they have a delicate, papery texture.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in colonies along water edges with leaves and flower stalks emerging directly from the muddy bottom or shallow water. No central stem - everything sprouts from the base like a bouquet.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened seeds clustered in round, burr-like heads that turn brown in late summer. The seed heads feel rough and prickly when mature.

habitat: Look for broadleaf arrowhead along the muddy edges of ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and marshes throughout New England. It thrives in shallow water or saturated soil, often growing alongside cattails, pickerelweed, and wild rice. You'll commonly spot it in both sunny and partially shaded wetlands from sea level to mountain ponds.

seasonality.spring: New arrow-shaped leaves begin emerging from the mud in late spring, starting small and gradually reaching full size. Early leaves may be more rounded before developing their classic arrow shape.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with fully developed arrow leaves and distinctive white flower spikes blooming from June through August. Flowers are most abundant and showy during this period.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back while brown seed heads become prominent. The papery seed clusters are excellent for identification even as foliage fades.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground tubers, leaving no above-ground trace. Look for old brown stems and seed heads frozen in ice or dried along shorelines.

funFact: Native Americans called this plant 'wapato' and considered its potato-like tubers so valuable that they were used as currency for trade between tribes - you could literally buy things with these underwater 'potatoes' that women would harvest by wading into ponds and loosening them with their toes!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other arrowhead species, but broadleaf arrowhead has the widest, most dramatic arrow-shaped leaves - if the leaf looks like a classic arrowhead you'd see in a textbook, it's probably this one. Remember: 'broad' leaf means bold, obvious arrow shape.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is also called 'duck potato' and 'Indian potato' because of its starchy, edible tubers that were a crucial food source for Native Americans and early settlers. The tubers are still edible today when properly prepared, though harvesting from wild populations isn't recommended for conservation reasons.
compareHints: Broadleaf arrowhead stands out from its relatives by having the widest, most pronounced arrow-shaped leaves in the genus - while grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, strap-like leaves and slender arrowhead has thin, linear foliage. If you see classic textbook arrow-shaped leaves emerging from water, you're looking at the broadleaf species. The white three-petaled flowers are similar across the genus, so focus on leaf shape for identification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's arrowheads, grass-leaved arrowhead is instantly recognizable by its narrow, grass-like leaves – all other species have distinctly arrow-shaped or oval leaves.
While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has broader, ribbon-like foliage, slender arrowhead's leaves are so narrow they look like green needles.
Compared to the common broadleaf arrowhead, Midwestern arrowhead has more narrow, elongated leaf lobes and distinctly shorter beaks on its fruits.
Unlike broadleaf arrowhead with its iconic three-pointed arrow leaves, sessile-fruited arrowhead has narrow ovals.
Among New England's arrowheads, arumleaf arrowhead is distinguished by its relatively broad, triangular leaves that are wider than they are long.
Among the arrowhead family, Engelmann's stands out for its extremely narrow leaf lobes and strict preference for acidic water.
Among New England's arrowheads, Spongy Arrowhead is distinguished by its uniquely soft, air-filled leaf stalks - a feature no other local Sagittaria species shares.
Among New England arrowheads, delta arrowhead has broader, more triangular leaves than the common broadleaf arrowhead, and much wider leaves than the grass-like narrow-leaved arrowhead.
Among New England's arrowheads, this species stands out for having the thinnest, most grass-like leaves - much narrower even than grass-leaved arrowhead.

Among New England arrowheads, hooded arrowhead is unique for its curved sepals that hood over the flower petals, while broadleaf arrowhead has flat, open flowers and grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the broad arrow shape.
